{{Short description|none}}
This is a list of some of the ordinary and [[generalized cohomology theory|generalized (or extraordinary)]] homology and cohomology theories in [[algebraic topology]] that are defined on the categories of [[CW complex]]es or [[spectrum (homotopy theory)|spectra]]. For other sorts of homology theories see the [[#See also|links]] at the end of this article.

==Notation==

*<math>S=\pi=S^0</math> is the sphere spectrum.
*<math>S^n</math> is the spectrum of the <math>n</math>-dimensional sphere
*<math>S^nY=S^n\land Y</math> is the <math>n</math>th [[suspension (topology)|suspension]] of a spectrum <math>Y</math>.
*<math>[X,Y]</math> is the abelian group of morphisms from the spectrum <math>X</math> to the spectrum <math>Y</math>, given (roughly) as homotopy classes of maps.
*<math>[X,Y]_n=[S^nX,Y]</math>
*<math>[X,Y]_*</math> is the graded abelian group given as the sum of the groups <math>[X,Y]_n</math>.
*<math>\pi_n(X)=[S^n,X]=[S,X]_n</math> is the <math>n</math>th stable homotopy group of <math>X</math>.
*<math>\pi_*(X)</math> is the sum of the groups <math>\pi_n(X)</math>, and is called the '''coefficient ring''' of <math>X</math> when <math>X</math> is a ring spectrum.
*<math>X\land Y</math> is the [[smash product]] of two spectra.

If <math>X</math> is a spectrum, then it defines generalized homology and cohomology theories on the category of spectra as follows:
*<math>X_n(Y)=[S,X\land Y]_n=[S^n,X\wedge Y]</math> is the generalized homology of <math>Y</math>,
*<math>X^n(Y)=[Y,X]_{-n}=[S^{-n}Y, X]</math> is the generalized cohomology of <math>Y</math>

==Ordinary homology theories==

These are the theories satisfying the "dimension axiom" of the [[Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms]] that the homology of a point vanishes in dimension other than 0. They are determined by an [[abelian group|abelian]] coefficient group <math>G</math>, and denoted by <math>H(X,G)</math> (where
<math>G</math> is sometimes omitted, especially if it is <math>\Z</math>). Usually <math>G</math> is the integers, the rationals, the reals, the complex numbers, or the integers mod a prime <math>p</math>.

The cohomology functors of ordinary cohomology theories are represented by [[Eilenberg–MacLane space]]s.

On simplicial complexes, these theories coincide with [[singular homology]] and cohomology.

===Homology and cohomology with integer coefficients.===
'''Spectrum:''' <math>H</math> ([[Eilenberg–MacLane spectrum]] of the integers.)

'''Coefficient ring:'''  <math>\pi_n(H)=\Z</math> if <math>n=0</math>, <math>0</math> otherwise.

The original homology theory.

===Homology and cohomology with rational (or real or complex) coefficients.===
'''Spectrum:''' <math>HQ</math> (Eilenberg–Mac Lane spectrum of the rationals.)

'''Coefficient ring:'''  <math>\pi_n(HQ)=\Q</math> if <math>n=0</math>, <math>0</math> otherwise.

These are the easiest of all homology theories.
The homology groups <math>HQ_n(X)</math> are often denoted by <math>H_n(X,Q)</math>.
The homology groups <math>H(X,\Q)</math>, <math>H(X,\R)</math>, <math>H(X,\C)</math> with [[rational number|rational]], [[real number|real]], and [[complex number|complex]] coefficients are all similar, and are used mainly when torsion is not of interest (or too complicated to work out). The [[Hodge decomposition]] writes the complex cohomology of a complex [[projective variety]] as a sum of [[sheaf cohomology]] groups.

===Homology and cohomology with mod ''p'' coefficients.===
'''Spectrum:''' <math>HZ_p</math> (Eilenberg–Maclane spectrum of the integers mod <math>p</math>.)

'''Coefficient ring:'''  <math>\pi_n(HZ_p)=\Z_p</math> (integers mod <math>p</math>) if <math>n=0</math>, <math>0</math> otherwise.

==K-theories==

The simpler [[K-theory|K-theories]] of a space are often related to [[vector bundle]]s over the space, and different sorts of K-theories correspond to different structures that can be put on a vector bundle.

===Real K-theory===
'''Spectrum:''' KO

'''Coefficient ring:''' The coefficient groups π<sub>''i''</sub>(KO) have period 8 in ''i'', given by the sequence '''Z''', '''Z'''<sub>2</sub>, '''Z'''<sub>2</sub>,0, '''Z''', 0, 0, 0, repeated. As a ring, it is generated by a class ''η'' in degree 1, a class ''x''<sub>4</sub> in degree 4, and an invertible class ''v''<sub>1</sub><sup>4</sup> in degree 8, subject to the relations that 2''η''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''η''<sup>3</sup> =&nbsp;''ηx''<sub>4</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, and ''x''<sub>4</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;4''v''<sub>1</sub><sup>4</sup>.

KO<sup>0</sup>(''X'') is the ring of stable equivalence classes of real vector bundles over ''X''. [[Bott periodicity]] implies that the K-groups have period 8.

===Complex K-theory===
'''Spectrum:''' KU (even terms BU or '''Z'''&nbsp;×&nbsp;BU, odd terms ''U'').

'''Coefficient ring:''' The coefficient ring ''K''<sup>*</sup>(point) is the ring of [[Laurent polynomials]] in a generator of degree&nbsp;2.

''K''<sup>0</sup>(''X'') is the ring of stable equivalence classes of complex vector bundles over ''X''. [[Bott periodicity]] implies that the K-groups have period 2.

===Quaternionic K-theory===
'''Spectrum:''' KSp

'''Coefficient ring:''' The coefficient groups π<sub>''i''</sub>(KSp) have period 8 in ''i'', given by the sequence '''Z''', 0, 0, 0,'''Z''', '''Z'''<sub>2</sub>, '''Z'''<sub>2</sub>,0, repeated.

KSp<sup>0</sup>(''X'') is the ring of stable equivalence classes of quaternionic vector bundles over ''X''. [[Bott periodicity]] implies that the K-groups have period 8.

===K theory with coefficients===
'''Spectrum:''' KG

''G'' is some abelian group; for example the localization '''Z'''<sub>(''p'')</sub> at the prime ''p''. Other K-theories can also be given coefficients.

===Self conjugate K-theory===
'''Spectrum:''' KSC

'''Coefficient ring:''' ''to be written...''

The coefficient groups <math>\pi_i</math>(KSC) have period 4 in ''i'', given by the sequence '''Z''', '''Z'''<sub>2</sub>, 0, '''Z''',  repeated. Introduced by Donald W. Anderson in his unpublished 1964  [[University of California, Berkeley]] Ph.D. dissertation, "A new cohomology theory".

===Connective K-theories===
'''Spectrum:''' ku for connective K-theory, ko for connective real K-theory.

'''Coefficient ring:''' For ku, the coefficient ring is the ring of polynomials over ''Z'' on a single class ''v''<sub>1</sub> in dimension 2. For ko, the coefficient ring is the quotient of a polynomial ring on three generators, ''η'' in dimension 1, ''x''<sub>4</sub> in dimension 4, and ''v''<sub>1</sub><sup>4</sup> in dimension&nbsp;8, the periodicity generator, modulo the relations that 2''η''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, ''x''<sub>4</sub><sup>2</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;4''v''<sub>1</sub><sup>4</sup>, ''η''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;0, and&nbsp;''ηx''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0.

Roughly speaking, this is K-theory with the negative dimensional parts killed off.

===KR-theory===

This is a cohomology theory defined for spaces with involution, from which many of the other K-theories can be derived.

==Bordism and cobordism theories==
[[Cobordism]] studies [[manifold]]s, where a manifold is regarded as "trivial" if it is the boundary of another compact manifold. The cobordism classes of manifolds form a ring that is usually the coefficient ring of some generalized cohomology theory. There are many such theories, corresponding roughly to the different structures that one can put on a manifold.

The functors of cobordism theories are often represented by [[Thom space]]s of certain groups.

===[[Stable homotopy theory|Stable homotopy]] and [[cohomotopy]]===
'''Spectrum:''' S ([[sphere spectrum]]).

'''Coefficient ring:''' The coefficient groups π<sub>''n''</sub>(''S'') are the [[stable homotopy groups of spheres]], which are notoriously hard to compute or understand for ''n''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0.  (For ''n''&nbsp;<&nbsp;0 they vanish, and for ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;0 the group is&nbsp;'''Z'''.)

Stable homotopy is closely related to cobordism of [[framed manifold]]s (manifolds with a trivialization of the normal bundle).

===Unoriented cobordism===
'''Spectrum:''' MO ([[Thom spectrum]] of [[orthogonal group]])

'''Coefficient ring:''' π<sub>*</sub>(MO) is the ring of cobordism classes of unoriented manifolds, and is a polynomial ring over the field with 2 elements on generators of degree ''i'' for every ''i'' not of the form 2<sup>''n''</sup>−1. That is: <math>\mathbb{Z}_2 [ x_2 , x_4 , x_5 , x_6 , x_8 \cdots]</math> where <math>x_{2n}</math> can be represented by the classes of <math>\mathbb{RP}^{2n}</math> while for odd indices one can use appropriate [[Albrecht Dold|Dold]] manifolds.

Unoriented bordism is 2-torsion, since ''2M'' is the boundary of <math>M \times I</math>.

MO is a rather weak cobordism theory, as the spectrum MO is isomorphic to
H(π<sub>*</sub>(MO)) ("homology with coefficients in π<sub>*</sub>(MO)") – MO is a product of [[Eilenberg–MacLane spectra]]. In other words, the corresponding homology and cohomology theories are no more powerful than homology and cohomology with coefficients in '''Z'''/2'''Z'''. This was the first cobordism theory to be described completely.

===Complex cobordism===
{{Main|Complex cobordism}}
'''Spectrum:''' MU (Thom spectrum of [[unitary group]])

'''Coefficient ring:''' π<sub>*</sub>(''MU'') is the polynomial ring on generators of degree 2, 4, 6, 8, ...
and is naturally isomorphic to [[Lazard ring|Lazard's universal ring]], and is the cobordism ring of stably [[almost complex manifold]]s.

===Oriented cobordism===
{{Expand section|date=December 2009}}
'''Spectrum:''' MSO (Thom spectrum of [[special orthogonal group]])

'''Coefficient ring:''' The oriented cobordism class of a manifold is completely determined by its characteristic numbers: its [[Stiefel–Whitney number]]s and [[Pontryagin number]]s, but the overall coefficient ring, denoted <math>\Omega_* = \Omega(*) = MSO(*)</math> is quite complicated.
Rationally, and at 2 (corresponding to Pontryagin and Stiefel–Whitney classes, respectively), MSO is a product of [[Eilenberg–MacLane spectra]] – <math>MSO_{\mathbf Q} = H(\pi_*(MSO_{\mathbf Q}))</math> and <math>MSO[2] = H(\pi_*(MSO[2]))</math> – but at odd primes it is not, and the structure is complicated to describe. The ring has been completely described integrally, due to work of [[John Milnor]], Boris Averbuch, [[Vladimir Abramovich Rokhlin|Vladimir Rokhlin]], and [[C. T. C. Wall]].

'''Spectrum:''' MSU (Thom spectrum of [[special unitary group]])

===PL cobordism and topological cobordism===
'''Spectrum:''' MPL, MSPL, MTop, MSTop

'''Coefficient ring:'''

The definition is similar to cobordism, except that one uses [[Piecewise linear manifold|piecewise linear]] or topological instead of [[smooth manifold|smooth]] [[manifold]]s, either oriented or unoriented.
The coefficient rings are complicated.

===Brown–Peterson cohomology===
'''Spectrum:''' BP

'''Coefficient ring:''' π<sub>*</sub>(BP) is a polynomial algebra over ''Z''<sub>(''p'')</sub> on generators ''v''<sub>''n''</sub> of dimension 2(''p''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1) for ''n''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;1.

Brown–Peterson cohomology BP is a summand of MU<sub>''p''</sub>, which is complex cobordism MU localized at a prime ''p''. In fact MU<sub>(''p'')</sub> is a sum of suspensions of BP.

===Morava K-theory===
'''Spectrum:''' K(''n'') (They also depend on a prime ''p''.)

'''Coefficient ring:''' '''F'''<sub>''p''</sub>[''v''<sub>''n''</sub>, ''v''<sub>''n''</sub><sup>−1</sup>], where ''v''<sub>''n''</sub> has degree 2(''p''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;-1).

These theories have period 2(''p''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;−&nbsp;1).  They are named after [[Jack Morava]].

===Johnson–Wilson theory===

'''Spectrum''' ''E''(''n'')

'''Coefficient ring''' '''Z'''<sub>(2)</sub>[''v''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''v''<sub>''n''</sub>, 1/''v''<sub>''n''</sub>] where ''v''<sub>''i''</sub> has degree 2(2<sup>''i''</sup>&minus;1)

==Theories related to [[elliptic curve]]s==

===Elliptic cohomology===
{{main|Elliptic cohomology}}

'''Spectrum:''' Ell

{{Expand section|date=December 2009}}

===Topological modular forms===
'''Spectra:''' tmf, TMF (previously called eo<sub>2</sub>.)

The coefficient ring π<sub>*</sub>(tmf) is called the ring of [[topological modular forms]]. TMF is tmf with the 24th power of the modular form Δ inverted, and has period 24<sup>2</sup>=576. At the prime ''p''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, the completion of tmf is the spectrum eo<sub>2</sub>, and the K(2)-localization of tmf is the Hopkins-Miller Higher Real K-theory spectrum EO<sub>2</sub>.
